pages.title: Objectives

objectives

Review medical bills and related expenses thoroughly.
Organize billing data accurately.
Summarize bills in a structured format to support a demand letter.
Identify and correct common billing errors to ensure the demand reflects true damages.

pages.title: Medical Bills
pages.text:
medical bills

are detailed invoices from healthcare providers showing the costs of treatment, procedures, medications, and services related to a client’s injuries.

In the context of Medical Summary and Demand, these bills serve to:
Document actual expenses
Support claims for damages
Verify medical treatment

pages.title: How Medical Bills Integrate with a Medical Summary
pages.text:
How Medical Bills Integrate with a Medical Summary

A medical summary condenses a client’s medical history and treatment into a clear, chronological narrative. Medical Bills contribute by:

Providing dates and providers
Identifying treatment types
Quantifying costs
Highlighting ongoing treatment

pages.title: How Medical Bills Support a Demand Letter
pages.text:
How Medical Bills Support a Demand Letter

The demand letter is the document sent to an insurance company or opposing party requesting compensation. Medical Bills are critical because they:

Establish economic damages
Add credibility
Demonstrate ongoing or future costs

pages.title: Why Medical Bills Matter in Legal Casework?
pages.text: Why Medical Bills Matter in Legal Casework?

pages.title: A. Establish Economic Damages
pages.text:
A. Establish Economic Damages

Medical bills provide a clear and measurable record of the costs the client had to pay—or became legally responsible for—because of the injury. These financial losses typically include:

Emergency Room treatment
Diagnostic tests
Physical therapy or rehabilitation
Prescription medications
Specialist consultations

pages.title: B. Validate the Injury
pages.text:
B. Validate the Injury

Medical bills help confirm that the client’s injury is real, documented, and directly related to the incident. Each bill shows that the client received treatment that is consistent with the type of injury being claimed, which strengthens the legal argument.
Injury → Treatment → Expense
This means:
The injury occurred because of the incident.
The client sought appropriate medical treatment for that injury.
As a result, measurable expenses were incurred.

pages.title: C. Support General Damages
pages.text:
C. Support General Damages

LOSS OF ENJOYMENT OF LIFE

EMOTIONAL DISTRESS

DUTIES UNDER DURESS

PAIN AND SUFFFERING

Client’s altered personal or professional duties can be inferred from treatment records and care frequency.

The bills reflect the severity and duration of the injury, showing how much discomfort the client endured.

Ongoing or extensive treatment can demonstrate how the injury limited daily activities and quality of life.

Repeated medical visits, therapy, or hospitalization may indicate psychological or emotional impact.

pages.title: Pain and Suffering — How Bills Help Show It
pages.text:
pain and suffering

Medical bills do not directly pay for pain and suffering, but they help quantify and justify it.

Here’s why:

1

Severity of injury

2

Duration of treatment

More extensive treatment → more severe injury → higher pain and suffering.

Bills over weeks/months → prolonged discomfort and disruption.

3

Intensity of care

4

Correlation with daily impact

ER visits, surgery, therapy, or medications → indicates trauma and ongoing pain.

Frequent bills for therapy or doctor visits reflect interruption in daily life, work, and recreation.

pages.title: Pain and Suffering — Computation Methods
pages.text:
pain and suffering

Computation Methods for Pain and Suffering:

A.

Multiplier Method (Most Common in Personal Injury)

B.

Per Diem Method

Step 1 – Sum all medical expenses
Example:
ER visit: $1,200
Surgery: $8,500
Therapy (12 sessions): $1,800
Medications: $400
Total medical bills: $11,900
Step 2 – Assign a multiplier (1.5–5)
Multiplier depends on injury severity, recovery duration, and permanent damage:
Minor injuries: 1.5–2
Moderate injuries: 2–3
Severe injuries or permanent: 3-5

Step 3 – Multiply
Example: Moderate injury → multiplier 2.5
$11,900 × 2.5 = $29,750 (Estimated pain and suffering damages)

1. Assign a daily rate of pain and suffering (e.g., $100–$500/day depending on severity)

2. Multiply by the number of days the client suffered
Example:
Pain duration: 90 days
Daily rate: $150
90 × $150 = $13,500

Per diem is sometimes used when the treatment period is clear from medical bills and records.

pages.title: Loss of Enjoyment of Life
pages.text:
LOSS OF
ENJOYMENT OF LIFE

Loss of enjoyment of life is a non-economic damage, compensating for:

Inability to participate in hobbies, sports, or social activities
Limitations on work or household tasks
Emotional or psychological impact from reduced independence or chronic discomfort

Medical bills and treatment records help demonstrate the severity and persistence of the injury, which shows how daily life was impacted.

How Treatment Demonstrates LOE?

1

Frequency of treatment

3

Type of treatment:

2

Duration of treatment

4

Associated limitations:

pages.title: Loss of Enjoyment of Life — Computation Methods
pages.text:
LOSS OF
ENJOYMENT OF LIFE

Computation Methods for Loss of Enjoyment of Life:

A.

Multiplier Method (Non-Economic Damages)

B.

Daily / Weekly Per Diem Approach

Step 1 – Sum all medical bills
Example: Total medical bills = $11,900

Step 2 – Apply a multiplier for LOE
Lower range (minor impact): 1–1.5
Moderate (temporary restriction): 1.5–2
Severe / long-term: 2–3

Step 3 – Multiply
Example: Moderate impact → multiplier 1.75
$11,900 × 1.75 = $20,825 for loss of enjoyment of life

Assign a daily or weekly rate reflecting the value of lost life enjoyment:
Example: $100/day × 90 days = $9,000
Or $700/week × 12 weeks = $8,400

Per diem is useful when treatment schedules and daily disruptions are well-documented.

pages.title: Emotional Distress
pages.text:
emotional
distress

Emotional distress is a non-economic damage that compensates for:

Anxiety, depression, or stress caused by the injury
Loss of sleep, fear of re-injury, or trauma from the accident
Social withdrawal or inability to maintain relationships
Mental anguish from prolonged recovery

Medical treatment alone does not calculate the dollar value, but records of ongoing or intensive medical care help substantiate it:

How Treatment Demonstrates Emotional Distress?

1

Intensity of care

3

Mental health treatment

2

Duration of care

4

Indirect effects

pages.title: Emotional Distress — Computation Methods
pages.text:
emotional
distress

Computation Methods for Emotional Distress:

A.

Multiplier Method (Non-Economic Damages)

B.

Daily / Weekly Per Diem Approach

Step 1 – Sum all medical bills (same as prior examples)
Example: Total bills = $11,900

Step 2 – Assign a multiplier for emotional distress
Minor: 1–1.5
Moderate: 1.5–2
Severe or prolonged distress: 2–3

Step 3 – Multiply
Moderate distress → multiplier 2
$11,900 × 2 = $23,800

Multipliers are typically justified by the duration of treatment, invasiveness, and client testimony or medical notes regarding emotional impact.

Assign a daily or weekly rate for emotional suffering:
Example: $100/day × 90 days = $9,000 Or $700/week × 12 weeks = $8,400

This works best if the treatment record clearly shows the time during which the client was suffering emotionally.

pages.title: Duties Under Duress
pages.text:
duties under
duress

Duties under duress refers to situations where a client was forced to perform tasks or obligations while injured or in pain, which exacerbates the injury or causes additional stress. This is considered a form of non-economic damage because it reflects:

Physical strain
Emotional/mental burden
Loss of normal life

Medical treatment alone does not calculate the dollar value, but records of ongoing or intensive medical care help substantiate it:

How Treatment Demonstrates DUD?

1

Intensity of treatment

3

Duration of care

2

Type of injury and limitations

4

Medical notes

pages.title: Duties Under Duress — Computation Methods
pages.text:
duties under
duress

Computation Methods for Duties Under Duress:

A.

Multiplier Method (Non-Economic Damages)

B.

Daily / Weekly Per Diem Approach

Step 1 – Sum relevant medical bills
Example: Total treatment related to injury = $11,900

Step 2 – Apply a multiplier for duties under duress
Minor: 1–1.5
Moderate: 1.5–2
Severe (prolonged strain performing duties while injured): 2–3

Step 3 – Multiply
Moderate duress → multiplier 1.5
$11,900 × 1.5 = $17,850

Assign a daily or weekly rate representing additional stress and strain:
Example: $75/day × 90 days = $6,750 Or $500/week × 12 weeks = $6,000

pages.title: Key Elements to Extract From Each Bill
pages.text: Key Elements to Extract From Each Bill

pages.title: 1. Facility / Provider Name
pages.text:
1. Facility / Provider Name

Examples:
Kaiser Permanente – Emergency Department
ABC Physical Therapy
Imaging Center of North County

Why this matters:

It identifies the type of provider (ER, imaging, specialist), which helps establish treatment flow and severity. Insurance adjusters also cross-verify providers to ensure consistency in reported injuries.

pages.title: 2. Date of Service (DOS)
pages.text:
2. Date of Service (DOS)

Each treatment date is crucial.

Why this matters:

Supports the timeline of injuries and treatment
Helps determine treatment gaps
Allows the legal team to argue ongoing vs. resolved symptoms
Shows whether treatment was prompt after the accident (insurers scrutinize delays)

In your documents, always list bills chronologically.

pages.title: 3. CPT or Procedure Codes
pages.text:
3. CPT or Procedure Codes

CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) codes describe specific services, such as:
99284 – ER visit
72148 – MRI

Why this matters:

Confirms the service provided
Useful when verifying medical necessity
Required when organizing treatment categories

Understanding CPT codes is essential for both legal and medical VAs because it helps you properly categorize treatment.

pages.title: 4. Total Charges vs. Adjusted Amounts
pages.text:
4. Total Charges vs. Adjusted Amounts

Bills often show several financial columns:
Total Charge (Billed Amount)
Insurance Adjustments / Write-offs
Allowed Amount
Patient Responsibility (copay, deductible, coinsurance)

Why this matters:

A. Total Charges (Original Billed Amount)
B. Total Amount After Adjustment

pages.title: 5. Confirming Client’s Desired Amount
pages.text:
5. Confirming Client’s Desired Amount

This is extremely important.

Some clients prefer the full billed amount, while others want to use the adjusted/lower amount depending on legal strategy, jurisdiction, and insurance rules.

A. Option 1: Use Total Charges (Without Adjustments)

B. Option 2: Use Adjusted Charges (After Insurance Write-Offs)

C. Why Clarification Is Critical

pages.title: Net Sheet
pages.text: net sheet

pages.title: Net Sheet — Purpose
pages.text:
NET SHEET

a summary of the client’s total damages—showing all medical bills, adjustments, out-of-pocket losses, liens, and the final net recovery the client may receive after deductions.

pURPOSE:

Helps determine how much the client can realistically recover during settlement.
Provides attorneys and adjusters a clear breakdown of economic damages.
Ensures demand amounts are supported by accurate financial documentation.
Acts as a reference when preparing the Medsum, Demand Package, and Settlement Strategy.

pages.title: Net Sheet Components — A. Total Medical Expenses · B. Liens & Payback
pages.text:
KEY COMPONENTS OF A PERSONAL INJURY NET SHEET

A.

B.

LIENS & PAYBACK OBLIGATIONS

TOTAL MEDICAL EXPENSES

Includes all:
ER visits
Imaging (MRI, X-ray, CT)
Specialists
Physical therapy
Chiropractic
Pain management
Prescriptions
Surgical estimates

Note: ALWAYS separate TOTAL BILLED vs. ADJUSTED AMOUNTS (insurance, PI discounts).

These must be deducted before computing the client’s final net:
Health insurance liens (ERISA, Medicare, Medicaid, health plans)
Medical provider liens
Letter of protection (LOP) balances
Med-pay reimbursements

Note: OBTAIN updated lien statements before finalizing

pages.title: Net Sheet Components — C. Out-of-Pocket · D. Lost Wages
pages.text:
KEY COMPONENTS OF A PERSONAL INJURY NET SHEET

C.

D.

LOST WAGES / LOSS OF EARNING CAPACITY

OUT-OF-POCKET EXPENSES

Document all client-paid costs:
Medications
Orthopedic devices
Mileage to medical appointments
Over-the-counter treatments
Lost personal items (e.g., glasses damaged in crash)

Include:
Missed work days
Reduced schedule
Inability to perform previous duties
HR verification or paystubs
Employer statement

NOTE: Must be supported by documentation to be included in a demand.

pages.title: Net Sheet Components — E. Future Medical · F. Non-Economic Damages
pages.text:
KEY COMPONENTS OF A PERSONAL INJURY NET SHEET

E.

PROJECTION OF FUTURE
MEDICAL COSTS

F.

NON-ECONOMIC DAMAGES
(PAIN & SUFFERING)

Document all client-paid costs:
Medications
Orthopedic devices
Mileage to medical appointments
Over-the-counter treatments
Lost personal items (e.g., glasses damaged in crash)

Based on:
Injury severity
Duration of treatment
Impact on daily living activities
Limitations backed by medical records

NOTE: Insurance may multiply medical specials or use per-diem method.

pages.title: Net Sheet Components — G. Attorney Fees · H. Case Costs
pages.text:
KEY COMPONENTS OF A PERSONAL INJURY NET SHEET

G.

H.

ATTORNEY FEES

CASE COSTS

Typically:
33% pre-litigation
40% litigation
(Add jurisdiction or firm-specific percentages)
These are deducted before finalizing the client’s net.

Expenses paid by the firm:
Police report
Medical records
Expert fees
Filing fees
Postage/courier

NOTE: ALWAYS verify with the firm’s cost ledger.

pages.title: Net Sheet — Sample Computation
pages.text:
KEY COMPONENTS OF A PERSONAL INJURY NET SHEET

1.

Scenario
Total Medical Billed: $32,000
Adjusted Payable Medical: $18,000
Lost Wages: $4,500
Out-of-pocket: $600
Expected Settlement Demand: $75,000
Attorney Fee (33%): $24,750
Firm Costs: $300
Health Insurance Lien: $3,200
Non-economic Damages
Pain & Suffering: $30,000
Emotional Distress: $10,000
Loss of Enjoyment of Life: $7,500
Duties Under Duress / Inconvenience: $4,400

2.

Computation

Economic Damages:
18,000 (med) + 4,500 (lost wages) + 600 (OOP) = $23,100
Projected Non-Economic Damages:
30,000 (P&S) + 10,000 (ED) + 7,500 (LOE) + 4,400 (DUD) = $51,900
____________________________________
Demand amount: $75,000

Estimated Client Net After Settlement:
75,000
− 24,750 (Attorney fees)
− 300 (Firm costs)
− 18,000 (medical payable)
− 3,200 (Lien)

= $28,750 NET to Client

pages.title: Common Issues to Watch For in Medical Bills
pages.text:
Common Issues to Watch For in Medical Bills

1. Duplicate Charges

A charge that appears more than once for the same service, date, and provider.

2. Missing Bills for Referenced Treatments

A treatment or procedure is mentioned in medical records or notes but lacks a corresponding bill.

3. Bills for Unrelated Visits

Charges for treatments, consultations, or procedures not connected to the injury or incident at issue.

pages.title: Best Practices for Addressing Common Issues
pages.text:
Best Practices for Addressing Common Issues

1. Flag suspicious entries

2. Communicate early

3. Document everything

4. Maintain chronological accuracy
